text: A distributed system does not begin with temporal logic. It begins with messages. LeanFM treats the observable contract as a formal language: which protobuf values may move, which actors may send and receive them, and which sequences are legal. Only after that language defines the possible executions do we ask temporal questions about every future, or about the existence of one future. This separation matters. The grammar defines what the system is allowed to do. CTL constrains the branching transition system generated by that grammar.

Begin with a typed message alphabet. A protobuf oneof distinguishes each message constructor at the byte level. Each constructor has typed fields and fixed field numbers. LeanFM adds a source actor, a destination actor, and a task to each message type. Thus an atom is not merely Fetch Command. It is: Gateway sends Fetch Command to Worker, for the get documents task. A decoded protobuf value is valid data. It becomes a legal protocol event only when its constructor, sender, receiver, and task agree with the declared atom.

A multiparty grammar composes those atoms. Sequence means that one event must precede another. Alternative means that the execution may continue through one declared branch. For get documents, the client first sends Get Request to the gateway. The gateway may reject it immediately. Otherwise the gateway sends Fetch Command to the worker. The worker returns either a two hundred result or a four oh four result, and the gateway sends the corresponding client response. The grammar accepts the success and not-found traces. It rejects a response sent by the wrong actor, a result before its command, and every message constructor absent from the alphabet.

Every legal trace prefix is now a state. Appending one legal event creates a successor state. An alternative in the grammar creates branching successors. Loops or retry rules may create cycles. The result is a Kripke-style transition system whose edges are legal message extensions. State predicates inspect observable facts: whether authentication evidence was present, whether the task is terminal, whether a response succeeded, or whether a queue remains within its bound. CTL does not range over imaginary behavior. Its path quantifiers range over the permitted futures generated from the current legal prefix.

CTL keeps path quantification and temporal position separate. E F p means: there exists a permitted path, and there exists a position on that path, where p holds. A F p means: for every permitted path, there exists a position where p holds. E G p means: there exists a permitted path such that, for every position on it, p holds. A G p means: for every permitted path and every position on that path, p holds. E and A quantify over futures. F and G quantify over positions along a chosen future. Writing the quantifiers makes the two coordinates explicit, and prevents the word always from silently doing two different jobs.

The message grammar makes concrete requirements possible. A G: success implies that authentication evidence was present, is a safety requirement. No legal future may reach an unauthenticated success. A F terminal is a liveness requirement. Every permitted future must eventually reach a terminal state. E F not found is an existence requirement. The model must retain at least one legal execution that reaches the declared not-found outcome. E G within bound asks whether at least one indefinitely continuing execution can preserve a resource invariant. These formulas constrain the same transition system, but they make importantly different claims.

The exact dualities also determine how LeanFM searches. A G p is equivalent to not E F not p. To check a universal invariant, search for one reachable state where p is false. A F p is equivalent to not E G not p. To check universal eventuality, search for one path on which not p persists forever. A counterexample is finite for the safety case. For liveness over a finite graph, it is represented by a reachable cycle or terminal continuation that avoids p. Universal verification is therefore reduced to an existential witness search followed by logical negation; it is not a request to enumerate every complete future.

A cryptographic protocol provides another useful message grammar. Imagine that Alice and Bob begin with identical Rubik's cubes and publicly agree on a move. Each privately rolls a die. Alice applies the move a times; Bob applies it b times. They hand the scrambled cubes to an untrusted relay called N S A, which forwards each cube. Alice applies her private move count to Bob's cube. Bob applies his private count to Alice's. Because repeated applications commute, both finish at M to the power a plus b, applied to the initial cube. They have matching states without sending either private roll. But this is only an intuition pump, not secure Diffie Hellman. Six possibilities are trivial to enumerate, and this construction adds exponents. Real Diffie Hellman chooses a large cyclic group. Alice sends capital A equal to g to the power a. Bob sends capital B equal to g to the power b. Alice computes B to the power a. Bob computes A to the power b. Both obtain g to the power a times b. The relay observes the public group, g, A, and B, but recovering a or b requires solving the discrete logarithm problem in the chosen group. The shared value is then passed through a key derivation function and used by an authenticated encryption scheme. Alice and Bob may exchange encrypted messages in both directions, but only with distinct nonces and normally distinct directional keys. In LeanFM, every public value, ciphertext, nonce, sender, receiver, and ordering rule belongs in the message grammar; secrecy, key agreement, freshness, and authentication are separate theorems over the permitted executions.

LeanFM combines temporal and alethic readings by interpreting possibility and necessity relative to the present and permitted future. Possibly p means E F p: p holds now or at some future position on some path. Necessarily p means A G p: p holds now and at every future position on every path. This is a reading of standard CTL semantics, with position zero included. Eventually is shorthand for A F only when the universal path quantifier is understood. E G is useful in finding the counterexamples to A F, through A F p equivalent to not E G not p. Pairing A F with A G gives an LTL-like vocabulary of eventuality and invariance. Under universal path interpretation, F p corresponds to A F p and G p corresponds to A G p; arbitrary LTL formulas do not all translate that way into CTL. English prompts become candidate actors, message constructors, legal grammar branches, and precise obligations that stakeholders review. Security protocols also motivate epistemic and doxastic modalities: Alice knows p, or Alice believes p. Permissions motivate deontic modalities: an action is permitted, or obligatory. Knowledge needs an information relation; belief needs its own semantics; permission and obligation need a policy relation. These additional modalities are design directions, not operators already implemented by the CTL evaluator.

The complete argument is now reviewable at three levels. Protobuf defines the values that resolve to bytes. The multiparty grammar defines legal communication between actors. CTL and Lean theorems constrain all states and futures generated by that communication, including requirements that are not themselves messages. A counterexample identifies a concrete legal trace prefix and continuation. A proof records that no such witness exists in the checked model. That is the role of CTL in LeanFM: not decoration after implementation, but precise requirements over a byte-level language of observable behavior.
